title: Information sharing to safeguard children: the s16LA duty and consent
blurb: Apply the statutory information sharing duty: what must be shared, why consent is not the test, and the one narrow exception.
question: In October 2026 a children's nurse in England has early concerns about a 6-year-old's welfare. Her mother refuses consent to anything being passed on and threatens to complain. What does the law now require of the nurse?

teach.body: Since 30 September 2026, section 16LA of the Children Act 2004 (inserted by the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026) requires relevant organisations in England to share information they hold that is relevant to safeguarding or promoting a child's welfare, where sharing may help another relevant organisation carry out its functions. Plain English: if what you know could help another agency help or protect a child, you must pass it on.
teach.cite: Children Act 2004 s16LA; Information Sharing Duty statutory guidance, Sept 2026

teach.h: The duty in four numbers and words

items.label: s47 or any other threshold need not be met first
consent is not required to share under the duty
applies from birth to the 18th birthday

teach.caption: The duty applies to information about the child AND about other people connected to the child, such as a parent's alcohol use.

teach.h: The three tests before you share

steps.label: Relevance
steps.sub: Does it bear on the child's safety or welfare?

steps.label: May facilitate
steps.sub: Could it help the recipient assess, decide, support or act?

steps.label: Detriment
steps.sub: Would sharing be MORE harmful to the child than not sharing?

steps.label: Share and record
steps.sub: What, with whom, why; be open with the family if safe

teach.caption: Statutory guidance para 14: relevance, may facilitate, detriment.

rows.label: Threshold
values: No threshold: early help and unmet need count

rows.label: Consent
values: Not required; do not ask if you will share anyway

rows.label: Confidence
values: Disclosure under the duty breaches no confidence

rows.label: Parent objects
values: Not a reason: must still share

teach.h: Consent is not the lawful basis
teach.body: Consent is just one lawful basis under data protection law, and it is rarely the right one here: power is unequal and consent can be withdrawn. Public task or legal obligation usually apply. Seeking consent and then sharing when it is refused gives the family a false choice. Transparency is different: tell the child and family what you will share and why, unless telling them would put the child at risk.

children.edge: Sharing would put the child at immediate risk
children.label: Withhold that detail only, record why
Ask safeguarding lead or Caldicott Guardian promptly

teach.caption: Withholding must be rare and is about detriment to the CHILD, not discomfort for the practitioner.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Leah on the children's ward
items: Leah, 6, is admitted with a chest infection. Staff notice she is often unwashed, hungry and frequently misses clinic appointments.
Her mother says she does not want 'social services involved' and will complain if anything is shared.
Nurse Priya applies the tests: the information is relevant to Leah's welfare and could help Family Help assess need. Sharing is not more harmful to Leah.
She tells the mother, calmly and honestly, what will be shared and why, shares only what is necessary with children's social care, and records what, with whom and why.

teach.text: Do not apply the old 'seven golden rules' as current law, and do not treat 'no consent' or 'parent unhappy' as reasons to stop. The single exception is detriment: sharing would be more harmful to the child than not sharing.

head: Covered
Examples
rows: Local authorities, ICBs, NHS trusts, police, youth justice
Young people once they turn 18 (other routes apply)
teach.caption: Unborn children: share per Working Together 2026; the duty itself runs from birth.

items: s16LA Children Act 2004 duty in force from 30 September 2026 in England.
Share relevant information that may help another agency safeguard or promote a child's welfare.
No threshold; consent not required; disclosure breaches no obligation of confidence.
Sole exception: sharing would be more detrimental to the child than not sharing (rare, recorded, reviewed).
Be transparent with families where safe; share the minimum necessary; record what, with whom and why.

summary: You can now apply the s16LA information sharing duty: share relevant welfare information without waiting for a threshold or consent, use the detriment exception correctly, and record and explain what you share. You can also correct the old belief that consent or parental objection blocks sharing.

A.q: A health visitor in England has emerging concerns about the welfare of Kai, 2, but nothing that suggests significant harm. Under the s16LA duty, what applies to sharing these concerns with Family Help?
options: The concern must first meet the s47 threshold
Sharing needs written consent from Kai's parents
Sharing is optional until a referral is accepted
Relevant information must be shared without a threshold
A.why: s16LA removes any statutory threshold: information relevant to safeguarding or promoting welfare, including early help and unmet need, must be shared where it may help the recipient.

whyNot.0: The guidance states there is no requirement for a particular statutory threshold such as s47 before sharing.
whyNot.1: Consent is not required to share under the duty.
whyNot.2: It is a duty ('must'), not an option, and does not wait for a referral to be accepted.

A.q: From which date has the statutory information sharing duty under s16LA of the Children Act 2004 applied in England?
options: 1 September 2026
18 March 2026
30 September 2026
29 April 2026
A.why: The duty commenced on 30 September 2026 and applies to scenarios arising after that date.

whyNot.0: 1 September 2026 is when the new immunisation schedule began, not when s16LA started.
whyNot.1: 18 March 2026 is when Working Together 2026 was added to GOV.UK, not when the duty commenced.
whyNot.3: 29 April 2026 is the reported Royal Assent date of the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act, not commencement of s16LA.

A.q: Under the s16LA duty, in which situation may a nurse decide not to share a particular piece of information about a child?
options: Sharing it would be more harmful to the child
The parent has refused consent to share it
The nurse fears a complaint from the family
The information concerns an adult relative
A.why: The only exception is where the practitioner considers disclosure would be more detrimental to the child than not disclosing.

whyNot.1: Lack of consent is expressly listed as a concern that does not justify withholding.
whyNot.2: Fear of criticism or complaint is not a reason to withhold under the guidance.
whyNot.3: The duty covers information about other individuals connected to the child, such as parents.

B.q: A nurse plans to share concerns about Amir, 9, with children's social care under the s16LA duty. She asks his father, 'Is it OK if I pass this on?' The father says no. What is the main problem with her approach?
options: She should have asked Amir's mother as well
Consent was needed in writing, not verbally
Asking for consent offered a false choice
She should now wait for a manager to agree
B.why: Where the duty applies and she will share anyway, seeking consent is misleading. She should be transparent about what will be shared and why, not ask permission.

whyNot.0: The issue is seeking consent at all, not which parent was asked.
whyNot.1: Consent in any form is not the lawful basis needed under the duty.
whyNot.3: The duty still requires sharing; advice can be sought promptly, but it does not pause the duty.

B.q: A school nurse shares concerns about Grace, 11, with children's social care under s16LA. Which record best reflects the guidance?
options: What was shared, with whom and the reason
A note that the parents gave their consent
The parents' signature on the referral form
A summary of Grace's full health record
B.why: The guidance repeatedly asks for a clear record of what was shared, why it was relevant and who received it.

whyNot.1: Consent is not the basis for sharing under the duty, so recording it is not the key record.
whyNot.2: A parental signature is not required and implies consent was the basis.
whyNot.3: Only information that is necessary and proportionate should be shared, not the full record.

B.q: A ward nurse learns that the father of Jamie, 4, has recently been released from prison for violent offences and is moving back into the family home. What does the s16LA duty say about this information?
options: It falls outside the duty as it concerns an adult
Sharing it needs the father's agreement first
It must be shared if it may help safeguard Jamie
It may be shared once harm to Jamie has occurred
B.why: The duty applies to information about any individual connected to the child where it is relevant to the child's safety or welfare.

whyNot.0: The duty expressly includes information about adults and other individuals connected to the child.
whyNot.1: Consent from the father is not required under the duty.
whyNot.3: The duty is preventive: no harm or threshold needs to have occurred first.

C.q: Maya, 12, and her mother live at an undisclosed address after fleeing domestic abuse. A colleague asks the nurse to upload Maya's full address to a multi-agency system that many professionals can access. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Upload all details, since consent is not required
Withhold all information until the risk has gone
Share the rest but restrict the address, and record why
Ask Maya's mother to decide what should be uploaded
C.why: This mirrors the guidance example: location details could put the child at immediate risk, so that detail alone is withheld or shared on a need-to-know basis, the rest is shared, and the decision is recorded and reviewed.

whyNot.0: The detriment exception applies to the address because wide access could let the perpetrator trace her.
whyNot.1: Only the harmful detail is withheld; all other relevant safeguarding information should still be shared.
whyNot.3: The decision rests on detriment to the child, judged by the practitioner, not on parental choice.

C.q: A GP practice nurse sees Ethan, 14, whose mother appears erratic and discloses heavy drinking. Ethan has never been known to children's social care. The nurse is unsure how significant this is. What is the best next step?
options: Wait for clearer evidence of significant harm
Document the concern and take no further action
Ask Ethan whether he agrees to a referral
Request information from other agencies
C.why: Where significance is unclear, the guidance encourages requesting information from other agencies to inform judgement, then sharing under the duty if relevant.

whyNot.0: No threshold of significant harm is needed; waiting risks missing emerging need.
whyNot.1: Recording alone does not meet the duty where information could help another agency.
whyNot.2: Consent is not the test, and asking Ethan to agree to a referral offers a false choice.

C.q: A nurse feels uncomfortable about sharing concerns regarding Isla, 3, because the family are well known to her and she fears damaging their relationship. What does the statutory guidance advise?
options: Hold back until the family consents to share
Seek prompt advice and share if the tests are met
Pass the decision to the family's GP instead
Share an anonymised summary without Isla's name
C.why: Feeling unsure or uncomfortable does not justify withholding; the guidance advises prompt advice from a manager, safeguarding lead or Caldicott Guardian, then sharing where the tests are met.

whyNot.0: Consent is not required and lack of it does not justify withholding.
whyNot.2: The duty sits with the organisation holding the information, so it cannot be handed off.
whyNot.3: Anonymised information would not let the recipient identify and help Isla.

reteach.title: Think of a jigsaw
reteach.question: Each professional holds one jigsaw piece of a child's life. Why does the law now say you must hand your piece over?

blocks.h: No single piece shows the picture
blocks.body: A teacher sees a withdrawn child, a GP hears a parent's stress, police hold history on a family friend. Alone, each looks minor. Put together, they can show abuse. The s16LA duty exists so pieces are joined early, without waiting for a threshold or for permission.

blocks.text: Transparency is not consent. You tell the family what you are sharing (if safe); you do not ask their permission.

explain.body: Relevant organisations must share information relevant to safeguarding or promoting a child's welfare where it may help another relevant organisation's functions. It applies to new and known needs, and to early help as well as protection.

test.q: Which description best fits the s16LA duty?
options: A power to share after a s47 enquiry begins
A duty on local authority social workers
A right for parents to veto information sharing
A duty to share relevant welfare information
test.why: s16LA imposes a duty ('must') to share information relevant to safeguarding or promoting a child's welfare.

whyNot.0: It is a duty, and no s47 threshold is needed.
whyNot.1: It covers NHS trusts, ICBs, police, education, GPs and others, not social workers alone.
whyNot.2: Parents have no veto; consent is not required.

explain.body: Consent is not required. A disclosure under the duty does not breach any obligation of confidence (s16LA(7)), so there is no need to weigh the overriding public interest. Be open with families where it is safe.

test.q: A nurse shares a mother's confidential mental health information under s16LA because it is relevant to her baby's welfare. What is the legal position?
options: It breaches no obligation of confidence
It breaches confidence unless a court orders it
It is lawful once the mother signs consent
It needs a public interest test to be lawful
test.why: s16LA(7): a disclosure under the section does not breach any obligation of confidence owed by the person disclosing.

whyNot.1: No court order is needed for sharing under the duty.
whyNot.3: The guidance says there is no need to decide whether sharing is in the overriding public interest.

explain.body: The duty does not apply where the practitioner considers sharing would be more detrimental to the child than not sharing. This is rare: for example immediate risk from disclosing a hidden address, or prejudicing a police investigation to the child's detriment. Withhold only what causes the harm, record why and review.

test.q: Which is a valid reason under the guidance to withhold a detail when sharing about a child?
options: The child's parent says sharing is intrusive
Disclosure would place the child at immediate risk
The family has asked for a formal complaint form
The receiving agency has no data sharing agreement
test.why: Immediate risk of harm to the child from sharing is the type of detriment that justifies withholding that detail.

whyNot.0: Parental objection on principle does not justify withholding.
whyNot.2: Fear of complaint is not a reason.
whyNot.3: A data sharing agreement is not needed to share under the duty.

explain.body: Share the minimum necessary, avoid stigmatising labels and untested allegations unless relevant, explain to the child and family what will be shared and why where safe, and record what, with whom and why. If unsure, seek prompt advice from your safeguarding lead or Caldicott Guardian.

test.q: When sharing under the duty, which approach matches the statutory guidance?
options: Send the complete record to avoid gaps
Wait until the child has agreed to it
Remove the child's name to protect privacy
Share what is needed and tell the family
test.why: Information should be necessary and proportionate, and practitioners should be transparent with families where safe.

whyNot.0: Sharing the full record by default is not proportionate.
whyNot.1: The child's consent is not the test under the duty.
whyNot.2: Removing identifiers would stop the recipient helping the child.
